Under the provisions of Standing Order 43, 1 ask for the unanimous consent of the House to move a motion dealing with an urgent matter of pressing necessity.

That this House instruct the President of the Treasury Board to table in this House his program of "pain-free" cutbacks before he takes any action on this matter, and that any plans he formulates should include a list of program and service reductions which would occur and a list of any contracting-out of government services which would result from the illusion of a government restraint program.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, under Standing Order 43 I am raising a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
Arising from the fact that active support from the new government for the Rehabilitation International Congress, which opens in Winnipeg in June, has been lagging, and realizing that our attitude toward the handicapped is often their biggest handicap, 1 move, seconded by the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Crombie):
That the government move immediately to amend the Human Rights Act to provide full protection against discrimination for Canada's disabled citizens, particularly in the areas of unemployment, education, transportation and access, and also take steps to broaden the definition of disability in the Income Tax Act in order to make independent living financially possible for the disabled, rather than having them dependent on expensive institutional care.

Obviously, every member of the House is pleased that Quebeckers have decided in a very clearcut way to remain within Canada and to seek their future within the federalist system. speechtext:
Madam Speaker,
1 have a question for the Minister of Agriculture. It relates to the very serious situation in western Canada with regard to the lack of rainfall. As the minister is aware, there has been a considerable lack of rain, not only over this past spring but over the past winter and the previous fall. This lack of rain has resulted, in many areas, in poor germination, a lack of water and a lack of pasture for grazing animals.
I know that the minister convened a federal task force in Regina which was set up to assess this situation. speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, yesterday, in a provincial referendum, the people of Quebec opted overwhelmingly for the continuation of the Canadian experiment.
It was under trying circumstances that the people of Quebec had to make this fundamental choice. The question forced them to affirm their allegiance to Canada by a negative vote whereas, being people of action and people looking toward the future, they would much rather have done so in a more explicit and more affirmative way. They were forced to say no to an impasse, to a negotiation which was doomed right from the outset whereas, as people of progress and change, they would have preferred to open even wider the doors to renewal and reform. That fundamental choice has often been very painful since in the passionate atmosphere in which the referendum was held, they were urged to dissociate and even to oppose on the one hand their loyalty toward their French heritage, which is fundamental, and their affection for Quebec, which is extremely deep, and, on the other hand, their sense of belonging in Canada which is indestructible.
1 must therefore commend, first of all, the men and women who had the strength to say no in spite of all the attractive features with which that political rupture, which would also have become an internal conflict, had been embellished. But 1 also hasten to express my respect to those who, having supported with such devotion the other option, must now find the strength to yield to the will of the majority. This referendum has compelled us to state where we stand but it must not divide us. I would like to remind both winners and losers that democratic life does not proceed only from the opinion of the majority but also from the expression and inclusion of the opinions of minorities. That is why changes and progress in societies that claim to be democracies are achieved through compromise rather than coercion. The fact that we have lived 113 years in a democratic system in Canada allows me to assure the supporters of the other option that their deep aspirations will be met by political changes, different, of course, from those they contemplated, and that they will

May 21, 1980
Quebec Referendum
continue to stamp the evolution of our society and to stress what makes its originality.
1 would like to express the deep gratitude of the House and of all Canadians to the leader of the No camp, Mr. Claude Ryan. As the leader of the Quebec Liberal party and thus as the leader of the official opposition in the National Assembly, he has become the one who rallied all Quebeckers who refused to give up their national heritage, the land of our ancestors. A tireless Claude Ryan travelled for months to every corner of the province to expound to his fellow citizens the exalting option he had proposed to them as early as February, 1979- choosing both Quebec and Canada. All along the referendum campaign, with a great sense of understanding and despite many conflicting points of view, he was able to mobilize men and women from all walks of life and of every political persuasion who wanted to stand behind Canada's banner. And I emphasize that beside him were constantly standing two former premiers of Quebec, Mr. Jean Lesage and Mr. Robert Bourassa. Their presence was the symbol of a continuity which, from Lafontaine to Cartier, from Mercier to Laurier, from Taschereau to Lapointe and, later, from St. Laurent to Lesage, has always mirrored that of a majority of Quebeckers. Claude Ryan follows in their illustrious steps and his contribution to a renewed Canadian federation will no doubt be irreplaceable provided Quebeckers give him the opportunity and the means.
You are not without knowing, Madam Speaker, for the very reason that you are one of them, that all Quebeckers sitting in this House actively participated in the referendum campaign. You are aware as well that all members from all parties and regions of Canada made things easier for us, either by relieving us of some of our duties or by gracefully agreeing to changes in the conventions which regulate relations between our political formations. To all of them I, therefore, extend my congratulations and the appreciation of a grateful Canadian people.
Madam Speaker, I want to stress at this point the essential part played during the referendum campaign by my old friend and colleague, the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada and Minister of State for Social Development (Mr. Chretien). I need not insist on the generosity, perception and political talents of the hon. member for Saint-Maurice, whose outstanding qualities have been at work daily in this House for nearly 17 years. By its very nature the referendum gave us the obligation, as members from Quebec, to take part in the campaign, as we were invited to by Mr. Ryan, but our participation had to be consistent and efficient. The hon. member for Saint-Maurice was in control over that and dicharged his reponsibility with exceptional aggressiveness. He could mobilize and stimulate us when we were in danger of getting either discouraged or overly confident. With the same energy and love of country he will succeed in animating over the coming months the renewal of our Canadian federation.

Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext: The presence of the Leader of the Opposition beside Mr. Ryan and leaders of other federalist parties on the hustings of Rimouski and Shawinigan during the referendum campaign was the living symbol of the unity and solidarity which bind all Canadians. With all his eloquence, the right hon. member for Yellowhead reminded the people of Quebec in their own language that the Canada which our opponents were attacking had ceased to exist, that the so-called status quo was a figment of the separatists' imagination, and that all Canadians from all parts of Canada were pressing for change.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext: The premiers of other provinces also played an important role in the referendum campaign. On behalf of their constituents they too assured Quebeckers that they were not only open to change but also impatient to renew the Constitution of Canada. With remarkable restraint at the meeting of Atlantic premiers in Halifax and at the meeting of western premiers in Lethbridge, and in individual speeches made by Premiers Davis, Blakeney and Bennett, all provincial leaders explained why a vote for sovereignty-association would lead to deadlock, why an economic association not founded on political unity could not be negotiated, and why the government of Quebec, no matter what the result of the referendum might have been, could not possibly have forced them to negotiate on that basis. In so doing the provincial premiers have done a signal service to the cause of Canadian unity.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
I would also like to pay tribute to the brotherly understanding and sympathy extended by Canadians in other provinces to their fellow countrymen in Quebec throughout the debate that led to yesterday's referendum. Starting from the early 1960s, faced with the turmoil of ideas, contestation and social changes that excited Quebeckers, Englishspeaking Canadians across the land did not remain indifferent. They came up with a question rather than a refusal: What does Quebec want? That now famous question, of course, reflected a somewhat disquieted incomprehension of the social currents at work in Quebec, but for the main part it spoke for the open-mindedness and understanding of our English-speaking fellow Canadians.
May 21, 1980



The past few years have indeed been trying times for the people of all parts of Canada. The issues raised by Quebec separatists were of critical importance to people in other provinces, since the very existence of our country was at stake; yet the nature of the referendum process launched by the Parti Quebecois tended to exclude them from the agonizing debate and to inhibit their participation in the campaign. There were times when many of them may have felt that Quebec had become a national obsession, to the detriment of their own needs and aspirations. There were times when the frustration and sense of helplessness of many may have become almost unbearable, but throughout this period of crisis people in other provinces followed the critical struggle in Quebec with forbearance, tolerance, patience and hope.
Ironically, one of the greatest tributes to the political maturity and democratic spirit of Canadians may have come from one of the leaders of the Parti Quebecois, the chief architect of the strategy of etatisme, Monsieur Claude Morin. "In virtually all other countries of the world". Monsieur Morin said recently, "what we of the Parti Quebecois have been able to do would have been illegal".
Indeed, where else in the world could a political party have openly advocated the break-up of a country? Where else could a separatist movement have had free access to the media, complete freedom to run candidates in any election, the right to form a government of a province, and the prerogative to use all the resources which our constitution makes available to a provincial administration to advance its cause?
Thus, Madam Speaker, all Canadians can take pride in yesterday's victory. It is not only the victory of Claude Ryan and of Quebec federalists; it is a triumph for Canadian democracy.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
We strongly hope and believe it signals the end of a long period of uncertainty, of doubt and strained relations between Quebec and the other provinces of Canada and between French and English-speaking Canadians. It marks a new beginning. It heralds a period of healing and rebuilding. By voting for Canada the people of Quebec have recognized that their fellow Canadians are prepared to listen to them, to understand them, and to meet their legitimate aspirations.
But Quebeckers have also shown that they themselves are prepared to hear what other Canadians have to say, to find out what their aspirations are and to help them to realize their dreams. We Canadians are now agreed on a common destination, and that was the fundamental issue. What we must now do is chart a new course and agree on a common itinerary toward that common destination.

Such is the profound meaning, the only possible interpretation of yesterday's referendum. The majority of Quebec voters have refused to give their provincial government the mandate
Quebec Referendum
to negotiate the withdrawal of Quebec from the Canadian federation even though they had been assured over and over again that that could be done while maintaining some form of economic association with the rest of the country. Those voters said no because they put their confidence in Canada. They said no because they accepted the assurances from Mr. Ryan of the Liberal party of Quebec, and from the other federalist groups in that province. They accepted the assurances from the premiers of the other regions of the country, from the Leader of the Official Opposition, from the Leader of the New Democratic Party, from all my colleagues in the Liberal Party of Canada and from myself that changes were not only possible within confederation but that the rejection of the option advocated by the Parti Quebecois would take us out of the dead end and allow us at last to renew our political system.
On the other hand, we know that a large proportion of those who voted yes did so not because they were in favour of independence for Quebec but because they had doubts about our assurances and felt that they would better promote changes by giving tactical support to the Parti Quebecois.
I base this interpretation not only on the polls taken before the referendum, but also on the many statements reported in the press these last few months and on the referendum rhetoric of the Parti Quebecois. Altogether, what Quebeckers expressed yesterday was a massive support for change within the federal framework. We cannot venture to ignore this will to change which reflects that of all other areas in the country and to fall short of the expectations of Canadians. This is why, on May 14, I solemnly undertook to launch the constitutional renewal and never stop working at it until Canada finally has a new constitution.
However, we would be deceiving ourselves if we were to believe that it will be easy to keep this commitment. We shall need the constant support of the Canadian people and their representatives within this Parliament. We are also counting on the support of all provincial governments, including that of Quebec. We shall all have to agree on the basic principles underlying our efforts. We have to be receptive to the needs and aspirations of all Canadians, to seek together for methods and mechanisms more effective than those used until now and to be willing to make every effort required to achieve success. For that purpose, I have asked the Minister of Justice to begin immediately a tour of the provincial capitals in order to obtain the views of the premiers on the best way to follow up on their will to change. As for us, our only prerequisites for change are the two which I outlined in Quebec as early as January, 1977.
First, that Canada continue to be a real federation, a state whose constitution establishes a federal Parliament with real powers applying to the country as a whole and provincial legislatures with powers just as real applying to the territory of each province. Second, that a charter of fundamental rights

May 21, 1980
Quebec Referendum
and freedoms be entrenched in the new constitution and that it extend to the collective aspect of these rights, such as language rights.
I had said at the time and 1 say again today that we consider everything else to be negotiable. What we want is to give Canada a new, modern and functional federal constitution which will enable our governments to better meet the needs and aspirations of all Canadians. This new constitution could include, if the people so wish, several provisions in our present organic laws, but, it will also have to contain new elements reflecting the most innovative proposals emerging from our consultations or from the numerous analyses and considered opinions that have flowed in the last few years from the will to change of Canadians. I am referring, of course, to the many proposals made by the Canadian government since 1968, but also to the Pepin-Robarts report, to the policy papers issued by the governments of British Columbia, Ontario, Alberta and by almost every province but Quebec, to the constitutional proposals of the Liberal party of Quebec, many elements of which could orient the renewal of our constitution if they were ever put forward by the political authorities of that province.
Having said that, we must look into the possibility of making progress in this direction without the co-operation of the Quebec government. This is why I asked Premier Levesque during the referendum campaign what he would do if the No should win and until now his response has been that he would accept crumbs of autonomy but with some grumbling. But Quebeckers do not want crumbs of autonomy or anything else. They have rejected independence, rejected sovereignty-association while massively calling for changes in Canadian federalism. In other words, Quebeckers will not be satisfied with crumbs because they want a brand new constitution and all other Canadians, through their political leaders, federal as well as provincial, have indicated that they also want a new constitution.
Is Mr. Levesque ready to accept this will to change? Are his party and government ready to put independence or sovereignty-association aside? Is he and are his ministers willing to participate sincerely, loyally, actively in the renewal of Canadian federalism or will they try to maintain the status quo in Canada in an effort to exploit the feeling of frustration which would be the upshot? Madam Speaker, only time will tell.
But that is the general context in which Mr. Chretien is undertaking as early as tonight a tour of the provinces. Once he has reported to me, I will be able to consult with the leaders of other parties in Parliament, to communicate with all premiers and advise as to the best means of achieving the renewal of the constitution. As for now, all I can say with certainty is that my government is deeply convinced that the constitutional renewal process must be undertaken promptly. As for us, we are committing ourselves to see that everything will be in progress before the summer recess.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I wish to begin my remarks in the House today by congratulating Mr. Claude Ryan and all the members of his team who won yesterday an important victory for Canada after an honest and strong campaign which showed a deep faith in Canada's future. I also want to commend the role played by my friend, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chretien), by the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and by all other members who were directly involved in Quebec by their actions or by their remarks in this House during the referendum period.

1 think that it would be well too to underline that many of the Quebeckers, many of the 40 per cent who voted for the "Oui" yesterday in the referendum, were people who were not at all lost to the federalist cause. Many of those who allied themselves proudly and enthusiastically with the "Oui" option did so because, for one reason or another, they had come to lose faith in the force of federalism. I believe we can prove that that faith should not be abandoned among those Quebeckers and among others. I believe it is important for Canadians across the country to know that a large number of the 40 per cent who voted for the "Oui" option yesterday are people who can be won back to federalism.
I think that we, particularly in this House, and those who serve in governments across the country, should recognize that the obligation is very heavy upon all of us to take a role of leadership in reaching out to those who, for a moment, lost faith in the viability of the federal system and to prove to them by our actions that there is a great deal of room for growth, a great deal of room for their aspirations as Quebeckers and as Canadians, to be realized within the context of a broad, large land.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Also if 1 may, I want to commend the Prime Minister for acting so quickly after the referendum to set in train activities which will move us quickly toward real progress on the development of a new constitution for the country. I am pleased that the Minister of Justice and Minister of State for Social Development (Mr. Chretien) will be visiting provincial governments. I would hope that he will not forget to visit the governments of the territories.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: Right on.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
In any consultations that carry forward, and in any machinery that is established, I hope there will be an opportunity for the elected members of the Yukon and Northwest Territories Council to play a full and an active role in those discussions.
We are dealing with circumstances now which have never before existed in Canada.
May 21, 1980



First of all, as the right hon. Prime Minister said during the referendum campaign, the main federal political parties, my party, the Progressive Conservative Party of Canada, as well as the Liberal Party of Canada, have both solemnly committed themselves to a renewed Canadian federalism. The same commitment was made by the provincial premiers who were unanimous in denouncing the status quo. We were sincere in making that commitment and I am confident that the Prime Minister and his provincial colleagues were every bit as sincere as I was when they called for a renewal of the Canadian federation. Madam Speaker, we must make the best possible use of the climate of sincerity and good will that now exists throughout Canada, and see to it that our common objective, a renewed Canadian federalism, is achieved.

The second circumstance that is new is that, for the first time in a long time, it is my view the public of Canada are now interested in constitutional reform. There is a genuine feeling on the part of Canadians, in whatever province, territory or region of this country, that it is time to bring our constitution up to date with the realities of a modern country. That is true and that is important.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Finally, a third circumstance that has changed and is significant is that this country, Canada, has changed in the last 20 years. It has changed dramatically. It has changed to the point where old constitutional arrangements no longer fit. In my view it is this last point which perhaps is most important-the old constitution no longer fits the modern country. That is true not just in Quebec but in other parts of Canada where real and profound changes have occurred in the last 20 years. We are not dealing now with an academic matter or a question of interest only to governments. We must bring our way of governing Canada into line with the modern realities of the country.
Constitutional forms are an important part of that process. We need a new constitution. I welcome the commitment made by the Prime Minister and the Minister of Justice which was reaffirmed here today. It is a commitment, which I share, to a new constitution for Canada. We need a constitution that is located here in our country, a constitution that can be amended here in our country, a constitution that guarantees certain fundamental rights, and a constitution that articulates a sharing of powers that is appropriate to a diverse federal country. We now have a climate where that can be achieved.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
But I make the point that more than the law and more than the constitution is at issue here. There must also be a positive attitude among citizens and among governments, an attitude which is consistent with the changes in law and the changes in form. Among the citizens of Canada there is developing an attitude of respect for fellow Canadians of
Quebec Referendum
different backgrounds and a growing pride in the diversity and in the strength of the Canadian family.

Perhaps I can speak more specifically of the changes that now exist in Quebec, that exist in the so-called Anglophone community in the rest of Canada, because I am very much impressed by the deep changes achieved outside Quebec especially with regard to the aspirations of the Quebec people and the respect for the French language throughout Canada. There has been a change, a new respect upon which we can build a great country in the future.

I must say, however, that while those attitudes have changed among the citizens of the country, it is not so clear that attitudes among governments have changed. 1 think it is important that we address that question frankly here today.
I want to take the opportunity, in the climate of good will and of near celebration that exists in this House today after the referendum results, to point out to the Prime Minister that it would be futile for the Government of Canada to be seeking to draw provinces together to discuss constitutional change if, at the same time, the actions of Ottawa on other fronts were driving provinces and people apart.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I think we all know that the sense of being a nation is influenced as much by conduct as it is by constitutions. The success of renewal will be based upon genuine respect for the other partners in confederation. It would be both unwise and irresponsible for the Government of Canada, or for the governments of the provinces, to perpetuate an attitude of confrontation, or to seek to resolve legitimate differences by methods which erode trust or make co-operation impossible.
Hopefully yesterday's referendum in Quebec will provide very real impetus to the process of change and renewal. But the desire-indeed it is more than a desire-the demand for change is not simply a matter of that referendum and indeed not simply a matter of that province. It is a desire shared by all of the provinces and virtually all of the people of Canada. That fact must be reflected in the agenda for change which this government now has a responsibility to place before the country. It must be truly a Canadian agenda not simply an Ottawa agenda, a Quebec agenda, an Alberta agenda or a Newfoundland agenda. Other provinces and other regions have specific proposals for change to which they are equally committed as Quebeckers are, and which they have a right to expect will be debated openly and honestly by all involved in the process.
Certainly patriation, an amending formula, and entrenchment of rights are legitimate subjects for our Canadian agenda, but so is resource jurisdiction, including offshore resources, so is communications policy, and so are proposals to make some national institutions more effective and more representative of regional realities and regional needs. It is not simply that we now have before us a rare opportunity, a rare

May 21, 1980
Quebec Referendum
atmosphere of openness and good will, within which to address the whole Canadian agenda. It is equally that we simply will not achieve a genuine or lasting consensus if some parts of this country or some regions of Canada feel their needs are excluded from the Canadian agenda or are given secondary status in national debate and negotiation.
[ Translation\
I was encouraged by the remarks of the right hon. Prime Minister when he said earlier today that except for the basic principles he mentioned, all the other matters are negotiable because, to my mind, that commitment is essential to the future of the constitutional renewal process, since hon. members of the House of Commons and the Canadian people throughout the land view differently some of the constitutional proposals.

For example, I believe the Prime Minister and I have different views about the contribution to Canadian unity of the consciousness of being a people like the Quebeckers, or of being a region like the west, or of being a province. I have a sense that he is concerned that these more local loyalties will drain strength from the larger community. I believe they are a source of strength. Some members of his party agree with me; probably some members of mine agree with him. But, that question must be addressed openly by all sides. We cannot let our work be limited by the prejudices of a Prime Minister or a Leader of the Opposition, or anyone else. We are agreed on the framework of the federal system. The people of Quebec yesterday in a massive and dramatic way indicated their agreement with a federal framework, and now we must build and go where the facts of modern Canada lead us in giving flesh and form to that federal system.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The Prime Minister has indicated his intention to consult leaders of other parties here, and 1 welcome that. I want to anticipate that consultation and make publicly one suggestion that I think should be very much on the agenda of change.
As the Prime Minister and as the House know, one of our weaknesses as a country so far has been our failure, at least to this date, to develop national institutions which genuinely command the respect of the whole country. Some progress has been made. 1 believe progress was made by the late Right Hon. Lester Pearson and his government with the introduction of the Canadian flag.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
1 am delighted to learn that today a Standing Order 43 motion moved by my colleague, the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle), regarding a national anthem for this country, was accepted.
But, Madam Speaker, we sit here today in one Canadian institution, the only one that has live and genuine roots in every corner of this land. Parliament itself can become the strongest genuine national institution, but it will not have strength until it has real power, and the tendency of the last several years has been to take power from Parliament and to concentrate it in parties, or concentrate it in government.
When we were the government, as the House knows, we introduced proposals for parliamentary reform which were designed specifically to increase the influence of individual members of Parliament, and consequently to expand both the range of advice available to government, and the respect available to this institution. 1 would hope that the Prime Minister will recognize that one of the ways to connect the parts of this country to the whole of this country-one of the ways to ensure a genuine sense of the Canadian nation-will be to strengthen the most representative and national of our institutions, the House of Commons itself.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I said frequently during the referendum campaign that the referendum itself was a question for Quebeckers to decide, but that the work of constitutional renewal was the work of all Canadians. Yesterday's vote in Quebec ended the referendum campaign, but it did not end the demand in Quebec for change; in fact, it reinforced it vividly and reinforced it dramatically. That referendum cannot and should not be used to silence the aspirations of Quebeckers, for in fact it was an expression of faith and an expression of those aspirations.
For the rest of Canada the vote yesterday was an expression of pride and belief in this country in which we can all joyfully share. It represents a demand for change in which Canadians have every reason to join and, indeed, which other Canadians have articulated in other ways for reasons of their own, or reasons relating to their own situations. That result in Quebec should be used, if 1 might employ that term, not to frighten or divide Canadians, and I am happy that there is no hint of that today, but to unite Canadians in a common determination to build a renewed federation which can make this a stronger country, a richer country, and a better country in years ahead.
That common determination, Madam Speaker, exists among Canadians; of that I am totally confident. Indeed, as is so often the case, in a very real sense constitutional renewal is catching up to the attitude of Canadians. Canada already has changed and the people of Canada know it. It has changed for the better in our new strengths and our new maturity. What is demanded now; what is fairly and justly demanded of all of us, particularly in this House, is a political system, a federal system, that recognizes the change that is about us, and shapes that change to the betterment of all of Canada.

The vote which took place yesterday, May 20, was but a date in a continuing process. It was by no means an end but a beginning, and now it is up to us in this Parliament and in the
May 21, 1980

Parliaments of the territories and the provinces of Canada to implement the changes which are being sought by Canadians all across this country.

Madam Speaker, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), as leader of the Liberal party, and myself, as Leader of the New Democratic Party, have frequently differed in the past, sometimes over frivolous matters, sometimes over very serious matters, but I want to begin my comments today by complimenting the Prime Minister on the very fine statement he made in the House this afternoon and, in particular, for his magnanimous address to the people of the province of Quebec and to every Canadian last night on television.

Hear, hear!
[ Translation]

Madam Speaker, the historical debate that took place in Quebec proves that we have already reached a level of political maturity of which all civilized nations of the world are envious. In spite of some deep divisions within the Quebec society and also elsewhere in Canada, we managed to express our differences democratically. I can tell you without exaggerating that last night we showed that we can get along together despite deep differences. The Quebec people deserve our admiration and respect. Personally, Madam Speaker, I would like to say to those who voted yes in the referendum that their message was understood. Quebec society must come out and do so by setting its own priorities, and that can and must be done within our federation.
Madam Speaker, I am, of course, very pleased with the result of the referendum. The Quebec people indicated clearly yesterday that they want to remain within the Canadian federation. But, as I said earlier, we must recognize, however, that this is not a vote for the status quo. Our federal system of course is not without fault. During that debate, all parties recognized that there was an urgent need for constitutional changes. All party leaders in the House pointed that out this afternoon. The polls indicated, as I have noticed myself during my visits in Quebec during the campaign, that the great majority of Quebeckers want changes to take place as early as possible. Canadians in other provinces must take up the challenge. All Canadians, wherever they are, must respond positively to that major historical event and the federal government must act and be perceived, not only by the Quebec people, but also by all the other Canadians, as a government out to promote the fulfilment of the people in all areas of Canada.
While it would be a mistake of considerable proportion to suggest that the grievances felt elsewhere in Canada, such as in the Atlantic provinces and in the west, are of the same
Quebec Referendum
magnitude as those in Quebec, it is nonetheless a reality that must also be addressed at this time of constitutional change. In approaching this constitutional change, the spirit must be one of reconciliation and imagination. A reconciling of the frequently conflicting regional and national claims with imagination could make that possible.
The goal must be to make whatever constitutional changes are relevant as a means of having Canadians, wherever they may be, feel more at home in their own land so that one can be, as the Prime Minister said last night, "at the same time a Quebecois and a Canadian".

Hear, hear!
[ Translation]

Fishermen in Newfoundland, farmers in Saskatchewan, miners in Sept-Iles and people in every region of Canada must see the federal government as an ally, as their government. This is our objective.

It should go without saying that on this day, while it is appropriate to stress the relevance of constitutional change, to achieve this goal it is also important to note that policies, programs and attitudes are of comparable importance both in the short run and the long run. It is not simply the case that the need for constitutional change is now urgent. I would also like to stress that the means are at hand for achieving this change soon.
Members of Parliament and other Canadians have before them the report of the joint committee of the House of Commons and the Senate of just a few years ago, the considerations offered by the present government when it was a government just a few years ago, and the counterproposals made by the official opposition and ourselves at that time. There is also the Pepin-Robarts report, and the results of the first ministers' meeting in early 1979 which reached substantial agreement on many matters. Then there is the beige paper prepared by the Liberal party of the province of Quebec. It would be a mistake or simply naive to suggest that all of these reports reach the same conclusions. Of course they do not. In fact they conflict on many important matters.
However, it is important to stress at this time that these reports do provide us with just about all the information we need and an analysis of the implications of different choices which might be reached, depending on the decisions we make in opting for one suggestion as opposed to another. Furthermore, there are areas in which agreement between the federal government and the provinces has been virtually reached or, at least, on which differences are not great. These areas include family law, communications and cultural policy, language rights, and changes in the Supreme Court. These areas, I repeat, are among those on which there has already been achieved substantial agreement. Therefore, they are among those areas with which we could proceed in the immediate future.

May 21, 1980
Quebec Referendum
During the referendum debate, as the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition have already indicated, virtually every one of the provincial premiers indicated that they favour early constitutional change. Therefore early action is not only required and desired, but it is also possible at this time. Matters on which agreement can be quickly reached should therefore be quickly settled. Once they are settled we can proceed to more difficult areas, resolve them as best we can in the national interest and regional interests, and give Canada, at long last, a constitution that is located in our own land.
Hear, hear!

Madam Speaker, our approach and attitude toward constitutional change will be of very great importance in and of themselves if we are to get the kind of changes that we think are desirable. Now is the time, above all, to rise above partisan considerations.
Over 100 years ago the various elements which were not yet Canada were in a state of crisis in this part of North America. Leaders at that time responded appropriately. The arch political enemies, George Brown and Sir John A. Macdonald, came together in an act of great historical reconciliation. Speaking in the legislature in June, 1864, George Brown explained-and it was difficult for him to do so-the reconciliation with a point which is so relevant to us in Canada today. He said that only the most extreme circumstances could justify reconciliation between himself and his old opponent and that the circumstances which required that were the crises that existed in many parts of the land.
The result of that reconciliation was the birth of a non-partisan approach to nation building. The nation which emerged, of course, was Canada. I would like to suggest that today we are facing similar circumstances and that these circumstances require the same generosity of mind and openness of spirit from members of all parties in the House of Commons.
There are significant matters which divide Liberals, Conservatives, and New Democrats. They will continue to divide us in the future. However, many of the basic constitutional questions-indeed, probably most of them-have absolutely nothing to do with party differences. If we do not recognize this fact now, we will fail both the best traditions of our respective parties and, more important, we will fail the nation, i suggest that we learn from the attitudes of Macdonald and Brown and make a most serious attempt to achieve constitutional reform and consensus as much as possible on a non-partisan basis.
Specifically, I would urge the Prime Minister heading a federal delegation, at the first ministers' meeting or when the time comes, to head a delegation which represents, not only the government party, but Parliament, while maintaining a majority of government members. 1 would urge, in the spirit of Macdonald and Brown, that the Prime Minister give very serious consideration to the inclusion of the leaders and perhaps other members of the opposition parties.
In this context I would point out that the other parties in the House of Commons have representation from parts of Canada
which are not represented in the government party at this time. Also, in this spirit, 1 urge the Prime Minister to make the same suggestions to the provincial premiers. 1 have raised this very matter with Premier Blakeney of Saskatchewan. He has agreed to take such an open approach with his delegation to any future first ministers' conferences.
Hear, hear!

I hope that a constitutional conference will take place this summer and that, when the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chretien) travels around this country-and 1 appreciate the urgency with which he is now approaching that task-he will discover in the offices of the premiers a willingness to meet this summer to get this needed constitutional change under way. Of course, it is early to predict precisely what should be done at that meeting, but it is unlikely that an agreement on a wide range of difficult matters could be achieved. At least if the meeting could take place early in the summer, say in July, a very specific timetable could be established and it could be expected that two or three months ahead and periodically for the next 12 months or, at most, two years, final and definitive decisions could be reached on the constitution.
I put forward as a suggestion that at least for the discussion of such an agenda, for agreement on such an agenda, a first ministers' meeting be called this summer.
In conclusion, Madam Speaker, 1 want to emphasize the spirit of the determination and co-operation that is now needed in our land, and co-operation is the essence. The road ahead will not be easy-we are all aware of that-but 1 am more confident than ever before that Canada will not only prevail but will survive.
[Translation}
Canada and Quebec will continue together on a common course toward a just and exciting future.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, 1 heard the suggestion made by the hon. Leader of the New Democratic Party. It is a suggestion which 1 believe had been made by a few of the premiers also, to hold a conference in July. Personally, and on behalf of the government, I would tend to be a bit more ambitious than that. I would hope that we would do more, if we have such a meeting, than establish an agenda and timetable. Whether they could be part of a delegation at a hypothetical conference or not I suppose would depend on the hypothetical question of whether or not we could come together on a common program for action. Listening to the Leader of the Opposition and the Leader of the New Democratic Party, it does seem that perhaps there is a common basis for action on several fronts, in which case I think it would strenghten the position of Parliament if indeed a delegation were composed of the leaders of all parties in this chamber. 1 would seek to establish this, hopefully successfully, in the course of the next week, after 1 have had a report from the Minister of Justice and have had occasion to discuss with both hon. leaders opposite.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege in relation to statements made by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin), last Wednesday, May 14. 1 might add at the outset that there were some who felt that my question of privilege related to a comment she made earlier in her statement, in relation to her use of French and my use of English and the hearing aid that I was using in that regard. 1 want to indicate at the outset that that was not my concern. I wear the hearing aid, of course, so that I can bring more comprehension to the remarks made by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan).

speechtext:
1 should like to take a brief moment, since this is the first opportunity I have had publicly to congratulate the minister on her return to office. Since I held that office for a brief period 1 know the kind of staff that she has available to her and that they have a reputation for good effort and dedication. It is in that spirit that I raise the following question of privilege.
This is a serious matter, because the remarks made by the Minister of National Health and Welfare on May 14 in response to questions relate to the integrity of one of the most significant, if not the most significant, social programs in this country, that is, the maintenance and delivery of our system of medicare. 1 feel there is a consensus in this House, and indeed in the country, that all problems related to medicare must be dealt with openly, directly, and honestly. The previous government's solution in this regard was to proceed with an independent review. We chose Chief Justice Emmett Hall to undertake that review in order that the solutions undertaken by this House would be reached only following extensive representations and consultation, not only with provincial governments but by all interested and all concerned parties.
As a consequence of the remarks made by the hon. minister, my question of privilege falls into three areas: first, misrepresentation by the minister of the facts surrounding the appointment of Justice Hall and the condition and resources within which he was and is conducting his review; second, the misrepresentation by the minister last week in the House on May 14, and indeed in the last Parliament generally, of her authority with regard to the Established Program Financing Arrangement of 1977, the legislation which governs medicare financing; and third, the statements by the minister on the same day in response to the same questions which seriously call into question the credibility of Justice Hall's review and her government's intentions with regard to its impending recommendations. Those are the three areas of privilege, Madam Speaker.

May 21, 1980
Privilege-Mr. Crombie
Let me deal with the first, the appointment of Mr. Justice Hall. In answering a question in the House on the Hall review, a question posed by the hon. member for Oshawa (Mr. Broad-bent), the minister pleaded ignorance of the details of the Hall review until her party took office again in the spring. That is the beginning of the questions reported at page 1061 of Hansard. Madam Speaker, the Hall review was not announced, appointed or undertaken in any shroud of secrecy. The terms of reference for the review were tabled at a federal-provincial conference of health ministers on September 17, and that was a public meeting. They were tabled publicly. Indeed, those terms of reference were later published in a number of both daily and weekly publications, not the least of which was the November 20 edition of the Medical Post which carried the terms of reference verbatim. I am sure it did not miss the minister's attention because it has a very attractive picture of herself and a fairly attractive picture of myself. It talks about the terms of reference in detail, verbatim. They were produced November 20. We were not in power a very long time, but if my memory serves me right we were still in power November 20.
Further on the terms of reference, the hon. member said, and I quote from page 1061 of Hansard:
-we asked many questions of the government to know what was really the mandate of the commission. We finally found out that the terms of reference were ten pages long, which does not mean anything, and covered everything under the sun.
It is not easy to discern exactly what the minister means, but I will repeat it because I think there is only one meaning you can finally take from it.
-we asked many questions of the government to know what was really the mandate of the commission. We finally found out that the terms of reference were ten pages long, which does not mean anything, and covered everything under the sun.
Allow me to be charitable and say that the minister has confused the terms of reference, which are two pages long and are very exact and very precise, with a ten-page communique which carried my remarks about the two pages of the terms of reference. The terms of reference, those two precise pages, were subsequently circulated to the provincial ministers for their comments. Following that process, those terms were finalized to everyone's satisfaction, including Mr. Justice Hall.
The terms of reference were two pages long, a very specific review. The most central, and that is why I have cause for concern, of those terms of reference which the minister claims not to have had knowledge of until she took office was a set of guidelines, requesting consideration of a set of guidelines for the principles of medicare-portability, accessibility, universal coverage, comprehensive coverage, public administration, reasonable compensation, and uniform terms and conditions. Those were the principles for the requested guidelines.
I might say that toward the end of November a letter was sent to all ministers of provincial governments, with a letter attached by me which again was made public. It indicated to those ministers that we were going to proceed with the terms
of reference which I attached to them. I will not read the whole letter. I indicated:
-I have made some alterations in style, without substantive changes. I have asked Mr. Justice Hall to proceed with the attached revised version-
Also contained in the minister's answer on May 14 in which 1 suggest she again misled the House, she said:
When we were in opposition, the party in power did not send us a telegram with the information pertaining to the commission, how much money it had, what its mandate was, and so on ... Nobody knew the amount of money made available; nobody knew the status of Mr. Justice Hall or the tools at his disposal to conduct a proper inquiry.
That is simply not true. On December 4 in this House the hon. member as she then was, the minister as she is now, asked me a question on the matter. She asked me if I would outline both budget and staff components. 1 have the quote in Hansard if she wants it.

speechtext: Give her the page number.

speechtext:
It is suggested I give her the page number. The minister will find it at page 1987 of Hansard. I did not answer that day. I indicated in the House an undertaking to the hon. member, as she then was, that 1 would provide her with the information that I had already provided previously to the ministers in the provinces and indeed that we had tabled in a public meeting. I sent that letter, and that letter contained the information which she requested with respect to the staffing and the funds available. 1 know she received that letter.
Therefore, Madam Speaker, I would like to conclude that the record shows that, on the first question of privilege, the hon. member did know the mandate of the Hall review prior to her resumption of office, and that the financial and human resources available to it were also known to her prior to her resumption of responsibilities as Minister of National Health and Welfare.
The second part of my question of privilege relates to the question of the minister's authority. Here I will try to confine my remarks the best I can to the statements made by the minister on the fourteenth. I am also sure that the record will concur that the hon. member recorded again what she said when she was in opposition when she demanded that the government of the day stop cash payments to the provinces in order to force the provinces to stop what she called the diversion of federal health funds to other areas.
The point of all that, and it is one we discussed in the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs, is that according to the established programs financing legislation of 1977-the agreement was negotiated and agreed to by the hon. member for Outremont (Mr. Lalonde) and the right hon. Prime Minister of the day-it was not within and is not within the minister's power to stop or diminish the cash portion of federal assistance without the consent of the provinces. That is as clear as a bell.
It is wrong of the hon. member for Oshawa to ask a question implying that the minister has that power and for the minister to continue the charade that she does, because it is of no help to anyone. According to section 28, subsections (1), (2) and
May 21, 1980

(3) of the legislation that took away the power from the federal government, it is not within the authority of the Minister of National Health and Welfare to alter the cash portion until after April 1, 1982, at which point the legislation allows for changes without provincial consent.
That is why the hon. minister could not take the action which she publicly stated in this House that she should because she does not have the power. That is the whole point of appointing the Hall commission, to make sure that power is not there, and it does no good for the House to be misled, even with the best will in the world, that that power does exist on the cash portion.
The third area of the question of privilege relates to what I think to be perhaps the most damaging aspect. I am hoping the minister will correct me because 1 think we share a community of interest in the final conclusion of the Hall commission report. There seems to have been a continuation of attacking the credibility of the Hall commission. 1 read the minister's comments on page 1061 where she says:
I must be cautious because we are talking about a royal commission of inquiry-
She concludes by saying that we are not talking about a royal commission of inquiry, and seems to imply because it was not and is not a royal commission of inquiry somehow it is less of an authority and will bear less heavily on the decisionmaking process of the government and indeed of this House. 1 simply want to give her an opportunity to correct that impression because, never at any time, was anybody ever suggesting that there ought to be a royal commission, and the record will show that.
The move 1 took as minister of the day was to appoint an expert to conduct a review of existing medical services legislation, with a view to improving it, clarifying it, and protecting and enhancing the principles of medicare. The minister today has an opportunity to state again her interest in doing these things instead of diminishing the credibility of the whole report even before Mr. Justice Hall has the opportunity to deliver it. Therefore, I would move, seconded by the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath):
That the Minister of National Health and Welfare acknowledge to this House that she did, indeed, know the information of which she professed no knowledge last week and that in these circumstances she should correct the record of this House.

there public hearings? We did not know whether the hon. member had this in mind.

Yes, the hon. member fell too, but what I am trying to say now is that I do not think there is any question of privilege and I think my colleague, the hon. member opposite, is reading things which do not exist. If I speak English I will be in trouble again because I will use the wrong word, but he thinks there are suggestions against the Hall commission or against himself as the previous minister of national health and welfare in his actions to "save medicare". He thinks this is being criticized or questioned. This obviously is not the case. I think the hon. member knows very well that we supported officially, and have always supported, both in opposition and now as the Government of Canada, the work of Mr. Justice Hall's so-called review. Past that point I could continue and answer for a long period of time each point made by the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Crombie), but I think it is irrelevant.
1 think the hon. member should know-and I am reassuring him right now-that once instituted and established, the Hall commission became the official tool to save medicare. Anyone with common sense, it seems to me, had to support the commission, which we did do, and will do. So I hope I am clear. It is all in Hansard. The hon. member said that last week I, at one point, said that I would speak French because the question is delicate since it deals with a royal commission and that a few minutes later I said it was not a royal commission. Let us not play with words. It was question period. I had difficulty expressing myself in English because
we were discussing matters which could almost be legal. The hon. member was suggesting that there could be a question of privilege, and I did not want to create any suspicion as to the way he handled the erosion of medicare by instituting a royal commission. We differ on ideas about what avenue is best. The hon. member knows that. We have said it often. There is nothing wrong with that. We differ.
We thought the route which could be taken should be different from that of a commission or review of the situation. This being said, I and my colleagues have the greatest respect for an institution once it is created, and the Hall commission is an institution to which added credibility comes because of the past work of Mr. Justice Hall regarding the creation of medicare in the first place and all his contributions to the development of Canadian policies in many different fields.
I will finish on the expression "terms of reference". I happen to believe, and I am not the only one, that the so-called terms of reference are very general. I cannot withdraw that or swallow it back. I feel they are very general. They could not be broader, and 1 happen to be pragmatic enough that if I had been the minister and if I had decided to have a "review" of medicare, I would have preferred more precise terms of reference. That is a matter which could be discussed ad infinitum, but it has nothing to do with the question of privilege. My past experience with royal commissions or inquiries of any sort is that it may be better in a case like this to have strictly defined terms of reference.
My predecessor, the hon. member for Rosedale, chose a wide avenue; let us put it that way. I quote from his so-called terms of reference as follows:
The review is requested to consider the extent to which the goals set forth in the "Charter of Health for Canadians" proposed by the Royal Commission on Health Services in 1964 are being achieved.
This is one sentence out of three pages I have in front of me. My copy happens to have three pages, and it was attached to the communique of ten pages.

subsubtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   AGRICULTURE DROUGHT CONDITIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is my intention at this time to introduce a motion under Standing Order 26, followed by a very brief statement in support of this serious motion. 1 ask leave of the House, seconded by the hon. member for Portage-Marquette (Mr. Mayer), to move the adjournment of the House under Standing Order 26 for the purpose of discussing a specific and important matter requiring urgent consideration, namely, the agricultural drought, which might properly be described as a continental drought, which includes the major portions of Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and the interior of British Columbia.
It is imperative that the implications of this developing disaster, now reaching critical proportions, and the appropriate remedial actions which could be taken, be considered on an urgent basis by the government and the House.
I should like to make a few brief comments about this very serious motion which I have just moved. To begin with, I would say that an agricultural drought in western Canada is not unusual in itself, but after many, many years and many droughts I believe I know that this one is somewhat different, and I want to explain why.
It is most unusual because it is so widespread, spreading from the interior of British Columbia across the three prairie provinces to the east side of Manitoba. It is only a part of the north American continental drought which includes all the northern American states and the portion known as the northwest corn belt in the United States. It extends much farther north in Canada than any previous drought, including the ten-year drought in the 1930s in which I was very much involved.
I would remind you, Madam Speaker, and the House, that the last emergency debate dealing with an agricultural matter under Standing Order 26 took place on October 31, 1974, when the subject matter was the beef cattle market price situation. I am sure there are members in the House who will recall that that debate was precipitated by a dramatic slaughter of Holstein bull calves shown in living colour on television cameras and taking place somewhere in the province of Quebec.
It was over three years ago that the last debate on drought took place in this House during a Conservative opposition day on May 3, 1977. On both these occasions the prevailing agricultural crisis was not nearly as serious and as widespread as the present highly critical situation, and I mean that most sincerely. That situation involves the entire western grain industry where, in many cases, the seeding of spring grains has ceased because of lack of moisture in the soil. It includes the grass and feed sector so necessary for our cattle industry covering 45 million acres in western Canada, and it even includes the northern forest fire situation which is so critical. That is another extension of this serious drought.

May 21, 1980
Finally, there has been no appreciable soil moisture since early last fall, and it is definitely true that in the winter we have just been through there was indeed a drought. What 1 am so concerned about is that we came through a winter with no moisture in our soil to show for it, and I see definite parallels to the situation that prevailed in the 1930s. 1 see a situation building up which could last even a few years, and that would be sheer disaster at this time. 1 know the situation is in Madam Speaker's hands and your hands only, but 1 feel there is some urgency here which warrants the special debate 1 am asking for at this time.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   AGRICULTURE DROUGHT CONDITIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext:
I thank the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Hargrave) for notice of his intention to move a motion under the provisions of Standing Order 26. He has given proper notice to the Chair of his intention to move the adjournment of the House under the provisions of this Standing Order.
As the hon. member knows, the Standing Order provides that the Speaker shall decide whether or not the matter which he raised is proper to be discussed at this time. I have looked carefully at the conditions set out in Standing Order 26 and in the precedents. While the matter, of course, is very important and of public interest, in my view it is not a sudden emergency.
Like my predecessors, I must consider that a proper matter to be raised under the provisions of Standing Order 26 must relate to a genuine emergency. The situation described by the hon. member is of a developing nature. In fact those are the very words used by the hon. member himself.
In support of what 1 have just said, may 1 refer members to a similar situation which occurred on June 27, 1961, when the then leader of the opposition, the Hon. Lester B. Pearson, moved a similar motion concerning the drought conditions prevailing at that time in western Canada and where Mr. Speaker Michener ruled that the matter could be brought up through some other procedures. The situation referred to by the hon. member in the precedent that he invoked was, in my view, somewhat different from the one that we are experiencing now.
In this instance I am sure the hon. member knows that the matter can be raised in committee where the estimates of the Department of Agriculture are currently under study, and of course, also there are other ways for the hon. member to bring this important matter before the House. Therefore 1 must rule with regret-because I know a lot of members in this House share his concern over the situation which is prevailing in western Canada-that the matter is not a proper one for debate under Standing Order 26.

Today we are giving second reading to Bill C-16, which I think is very appropriate after yesterday's referendum vote of Quebeckers in favour of Canada. This bill illustrates one of the roles of the federal government for Canadians, namely, the redistribution of wealth which, because it varies according to economic times, plays in favour of every Canadian wherever he or she lives in Canada at one point or another in our history.
As many members sitting here today will recall, this is not the first time that we have brought before the House a bill very similar in nature to Bill C-16. Just over a year and a half ago, we discussed and passed unanimously, if 1 remember well, Bill C-20 which gave senior citizens receiving the G1S supplement and living alone an increase of $20 a month, which was divided for couples, each receiving $10 a month. Today's bill presents the same characteristics except that the amount of money is different. It is far more generous than the earlier one, but it serves the same purpose. It narrows the poverty gap in Canada, of course, for senior citizens in this particular case. In other words, it improves the economic situation of those elderly Canadians who are in the greatest need.
We decided that of all those in need of assistance in Canada right now, priority should be given to those most in need, that is, the beneficiaries of the guaranteed income supplement program and the spouse's allowance program.

1 think that all hon. members know that the old age pension supplement is paid to pensioners who receive the basic universal pension but who do not have any other income or who only have a small income in addition to their basic pension. The supplement is also paid to the spouse of a pensioner, aged 60 to 65, when the couple is in need. In other words, those who get the old age security pension supplement need some help and experience difficulty in making both ends meet. Of course, for several years now, more specifically since 1973, the old age security pension and its supplement are indexed every three months. But the fact remains that this is not an increase. Indexing is merely a means of keeping the pension up to date and protecting the purchasing power of the dollar or the income supplement.
Old Age Security Act
At the present time in Canada single pensioners, that is persons who are seperated, divorced, single, widowers or widows, are guaranteed a monthly income of $340.15. By guaranteed, I mean that if a pensioner, man or woman, in Canada depends exclusively on public funds to live and has not other personal income, he or she will get, under the law, $340.15 a month from the federal government. If that person has other income, for instance, interest from a savings account or a pension under the Quebec Pension Plan of the corresponding Canadian plan, then he or she can have a total income exceeding the guaranteed minimum. And that, due to the fact that instead of suddenly cutting off the pensioners from the guaranteed income, we have through the years adopted a scale to which people conform and through which we check the amount of their additional income. I believe everyone knows the rules of the game, that is, for every dollar of additional income from sources other than the old age pension, the pensioner loses 50 cents of the guaranteed income while naturally keeping the other 50 cents.
The amounts guaranteed the aged who are in need are clearly inadequate. On an annual basis, the amount guaranteed by our old age security programs, that is, the basic pension plus the old age supplement combined, represents roughly 80 per cent of the amount Statistics Canada defines as the poverty line. There is no doubt that an income which is slightly lower than 80 per cent of the poverty line is not acceptable in a country as rich as ours and is certainly not enough to live on decently.
The officials of my department estimate that there are approximately 700,000 single, widowed and divorced GIS recipients of the supplement to the pension who are living in poverty. Fully 60 per cent of them are women. Let me refer to a recent report by the National Council of Welfare describing what life is like for these women.
