You had the same in your speech, and that is very good. I am speaking of the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Crombie), my predecessor, because it is really important in today's Canada, it seems to me, to impress upon people again and again the effect of poverty, which is unfortunately often forgotten.
In this report we have one part of the testimony of a 67-year old "Mary S.", who said:
"I'll tell you what it's like being an old woman alone who's only got the government pension to live on . . . It's wearing out your second-hand shoes going from one store to another trying to find the cheapest cuts of meat. It's hating having to buy toilet tissue or soap or tooth paste, because you can't cat it. It's picking the marked-down fruits and vegetables from the half-rotting stuff in the back of the stores that used to be given away to farmers to feed their animals. "We live in fear. Fear of the future, or more illness, less money, less pride. Fear that the cheque won't arrive and we won't be able to work our way through the red tape in time to pay our rent. Fear that we will run out of food before the next cheque comes in.*'

May 21, 1980
Old Age Security Act
There is no need to say that this is not acceptable to me, and it is not acceptable to the Government of Canada that persons who have given all their lives to working hard, to raising families and to building this country, should have to live this way. It is not acceptable, and that is why this bill is among the very first items to be brought before this session of Parliament.
I know there will be some persons who will say that the situation is not as bad as I have portrayed it. They will say that not all single, widowed and divorced GIS recipients have incomes below the poverty level. Of course, it is true that those who have some outside income and who receive what we call a partial GIS, or a partial supplement, may have in total an income that takes them just above the poverty line. But, it is also true that many single pensioners do not have such outside income. The fact that there are 700,000 GIS recipients in poverty is proof of this. We must help these 700,000 elderly Canadians as well as those who are just at or above the poverty line, under which I am sure none of us would like to live. [Translation]
So the increase of $35 a month proposed in Bill C-16 will allow us to help them. Of course, the amount of money-and I anticipate, of course, the unanimous agreement of all parties- voted by the House of Commons, the amount of $35, will be added to the cheque for the month of July of unattached pensioners, that is single, separated, divorced, and widowed pensioners. So the cheque for the month of July will include the basic old age pension payment, the present supplement, the quarterly indexing-because July 1 is a date of quarterly indexing-and a full $35. I do want to make that clear for all those who are listening. I wpuld add that couples receiving a supplement, whether part or all of the supplement, will have $17.50 each added to their cheque, which makes a total of $35 for a couple.
So, in making that adjustment, what are we doing in terms of fighting poverty since that is the concept underlying this bill? In paying that supplement, we are bringing single pensioners receiving a supplement to their old age pension to about 83 per cent of what is called the poverty line. That is not ideal; there will remain a gap to be filled that we will indeed fill as soon as the economy gets going again. But it is still important to know that this year the July increase will bring single pensioners to about 83 per cent of the poverty line while next year will bring them to 85 per cent of the same poverty line since people will be getting it during the whole year, not only part of the year as in 1980, and it will be indexed every three months.
Now, with respect to couples, here is how the bill will affect their lives. Couples receive a guaranteed income, that is guaranteed for all those who do not have other sources of income, of $628.62 a month. So one can say that their income is equal to the poverty line; it is not below the poverty line like in the case of single pensioners, it is right at the poverty line-one could say that they are 100 per cent at the poverty line. The increase of $35 a couple or $17.50 for each pensioner will
bring them slightly above the poverty line, or about 3 per cent above what is considered the poverty line. Couples will therefore receive an annual guaranteed income of $8,162 beginning in July. It is easy to see from the tables of Statistics Canada that this amount is slightly above the poverty line. 1 believe that we can conclude on this point that bringing these people just above the poverty line is a very modest recognition of the role they have played in Canadian society. We are not talking about a luxury, but about a standard of living that none of us would ever accept and tiiat we are constantly trying to improve.
1 therefore think that I have explained how the life of single people and of couples will be improved beginning in July. I could add for clarification purposes that those who now receive the spouse's allowance will also receive the supplementary amount provided by this bill. Hon. members will immediately note that couples are treated differently from single people. Why is this? Does this constitute discrimination? I do not think so. During consideration of the previous bill a year and a half ago, we introduced for the first time the concept that couples would receive the equivalent of half of the amount proposed for single people. In other words, couples receive for both spouses the same as single persons. Why is this? The history of old age security pensions in Canada shows that, throughout the years, as our policy has developed, we have treated pensioners as individuals. It is now recognized that families have special budget problems and that a single person needs about two-thirds of the budget of a couple and not half as it was long believed. We must therefore increase proportionately the pensions of single persons, which explains the differentiation made in this bill.
Now that I have defined the basic amounts granted to pensioners and what this will mean in the fight against poverty in Canada, 1 believe that it is important to note that since we are increasing the cheques of all recipients of the old age supplement, whether this supplement be total or partial, we are automatically changing the income scale against which private income must be compared to determine whether a recipient is eligible for the supplement or not. By raising the income scale for all Canadian pensioners we automatically allow, as happened in 1979 with the previous hike, some 45,000 pensioners who do not now get the supplement because their meagre revenues are slightly above mark, to become eligible for part of the supplement. I would therefore invite Canadians who will be made aware of that by a special stuffer sent with the July cheque, if they have very low incomes, to see whether they will become eligible for a monthly supplement which, of course, in their cases will be less than $35 a month because it will be a matter of making up for their very slight income deficiency.
May 21, 1980

I shall now describe the cost of the bill which we are debating. Bill C-16 increases the supplement to pensioners by $35 per month. The cost in the first year of operation will be $345 million in addition to the regular program costs of the old age security program in the fiscal year 1980-81. In the first full fiscal year, 1981-82, the additional cost will be approximately $525 million.
The federal government is not the only source of financial assistance to elderly Canadians. It is fair to say that more and more provinces are introducing supplementary programs to assist elderly Canadians. Does this bill affect such programs and what is the relationship between the provincial programs and the federal program? When this House debated Bill C-20 a year and a half ago, hon. members of all parties learned for the first time that, in order to make sure that elderly Canadians living in provincial institutions around the country receive the full benefit of this increase which we are discussing today, a positive decision must be made in that direction by each provincial government.
Consequently, I have written to my provincial counterparts asking that they ensure that pensioners who receive what is called "provincial top-up payments" receive the full benefit of our federal increase. At the same time I have also urged that this principle apply, as far as is possible, in relation to the so called "comforts allowances" availalble to pensioners residing in institutions. I am pleased to inform the House that the government of British Columbia and the government of Nova Scotia-a province on the Atlantic coast and a province on the Pacific coast-have advised me that they will be passing on the full increase to all GIS recipients.
We are pleased and hopeful that the other provinces will respond to my appeal in a similar manner. There is no need to say that I will do everything in my power to guarantee that all Canadians eligible for the GIS or the spouse's allowance will benefit from this increase.

This matter is very serious indeed and I feel I have a duty to impress upon the House the need for a common approach throughout Canada and in every political party, because it is a fact of our democratic life that no single party represents each and every Canadian province, in order to settle the unfortunate situation of income pensioners living in institutions in various provinces.
Let us take for instance my own province of Quebec. Should the Quebec government-which, unfortunately, like seven other provinces, has yet to answer-decide in cabinet not to give the full $35 by increasing the comfort allowance, that province will pocket some $7 million of pensioners' money.
I think that that is quite serious and that members from all provinces should question the slowness which seems to exist everywhere, in order to encourage the provinces to take the proper decision so that pensioners residing in institutions can
Old Age Security Act
benefit directly from the increase provided by this bill concerning the guaranteed income supplement.

I guess it is fair to say that passage of Bill C-16 will present an important step toward assuring all Canada's elderly of the adequate income to which they should be entitled. It is not the only step we intend to take and, as I said, it is not the final step we have to take. Some money will still be missing to bring people living alone above the poverty line. An annual injection of more than half a billion dollars into the incomes of senior citizens in Canada who are in need is an important additional step toward narrowing the gap and relieving poverty in our country.
[DOT] -l
We should like, as we announced in the Speech from the Throne, to convene a national pensions conference, hopefully in the fall, and we would like this conference to bring together representatives of all the economic partners involved in the pension field. I am thinking of the private pension field in particular. There are the federal and provincial governments as employers and legislators, the private pension industry, Canadian workers and their employers, pension groups and other interested parties in this country. We want to know their views on the urgent pension problems facing the country and we want to discuss the issues of concern to them.
We have about one dozen very good reports and we are waiting for the Ontario royal commission report which was due some time ago. It is coming, and I understand it will be so thorough that it may comprise ten volumes. We will have from different sources, from the Ontario government, the Quebec government with the Cofirentes, from the Economic Council of Canada, the National Welfare Council and many other sources, such as the Lazar report, a reservoir of ideas that we must air together and discuss, delineating the avenues through which the whole pension system in Canada can be upgraded to ensure that senior citizens not only have the minimum-which we do not think is enough-but that when they reach the age of 65 they have the good life that they have slowly built through the latter part of their lives.
In concluding my speech, Mr. Speaker, I would ask for the co-operation of members of all parties for rapid passage of what I am sure is an uncontroversial bill, Bill C-16. It is only a beginning in this new session of Parliament, a concrete start toward the fulfilment of a promise for a better quality of life for the people of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, today follows a very historic day in which the people of Quebec decided that their future was with Canada and decided to nurture their roots dating back more than a century. I want to say to the senior citizens who made this country that they can be assured and proud that we decided yesterday in my home province, Quebec, and all of Canada knows and is discussing this vote today, to keep the heritage intact and to leave it in full to our children.

May 21, 1980
Old Age Security Act

Mr. Speaker, first of all I should like to thank you for the opportunity to intevene with respect to this piece of legislation. Like the minister and, indeed, all members of the Elouse, I am interested in its speedy passage. I do not think there is anyone who would oppose the bill. I should like also to associate myself with the remarks of the minister with respect to this being an example of the role of the federal government.
f was careful to note that throughout the referendum debate when questions of social policy came up, whether or not they should be shared responsibilities or the sole responsibility of a province or the federal government, very often people were quick to say that social policies ought to be with the provinces. I noticed during the referendum debate that the minister, and indeed the leader of the federalist forces in the province of Quebec, indicated on a number of occasions that it was concern for family allowances, old age security and social policies that come from the federal government, that weighed heavily on the minds of a number of people in the province. 1 think it would be worth while keeping an eye on what happens to social policy over the next couple of years with respect to constitutional talks.
I am one of those who believe there is a proper and appropriate role for the federal government in the field of social policy, both for the amelioration of the range of incomes but more particularly in funding of specific social programs. I am not sure how many in this House agree with that view, but it was something I had hoped to hear the minister mention.
Toward the end of her comments the minister indicated the necessity of provincial co-operation so that there is not what is known in the social welfare legislation business as any "leakage" to the provinces. The minister is quite correct; that can be a problem. I wish her well in discussions with the provinces and if she needs assistance we will be happy to offer it. Everyone here wants to make sure that funds go to those who need them.
1 was careful to note what the bill means to numbers of people. This is a very impressive list of statistics. The $35 increase in the proposal would affect an estimated 721,000 single beneficiaries, 225,000 married couples where both are pensioners, 44,000 one-pensioner couples and 81,000 couples receiving the spouse's allowance-in total, approximately 1.1 million households would receive the $35 increase.
The proposed increase of $35 per household per month, effective July 1, 1980, will ultimately amount to $475 million.
1 think anyone reading those statistics would be impressed that $35 seemingly goes so far, and 1 have some comments to make in that regard. 1 think it is well to put the bill in some kind of perspective, and a historical perspective is always wise.
In 1967 when the GIS was introduced, a single individual received payments equal to 72.2 per cent of the poverty line. That is to say, when the GIS was first introduced we gave enough so that people were brought up to 72 per cent of the poverty line, or 28 per cent below it. That was 13 years ago.
In 1971 the GIS was increased by $20 per month. Without that increase an individual would have been at 68 per cent of the poverty line, but the increase brought him to 77 per cent of it. By 1978 individuals had fallen to 73.5 per cent of the poverty line with the low income they received from government pension plans. By April, 1979, with an increase of another $20 to the GIS, individuals were at 78.5 per cent of the poverty line. Had the boost not occurred, they would have been back down to 73 per cent. 1 am sure you could keep those figures in your head, Mr. Speaker, but others did not.
The point is clear. The indexing of the GIS does not work. That is why there needs to be a constant pumping in of fixed amounts of money. The $35 now and the $20 previously were not add-ons. In fact the total effect of the legislation since 1967 has been to maintain them below the poverty line and have their heads just above water. I know the minister is interested in bringing them up to the poverty line, and even beyond in the case of marrieds in the plan.
The fact is that the way in which we have gone about the implementation of the GIS over 13 years, every time we increased it, it has been purely to keep them where they were at and marginally more. The minister chose her words when she said "narrowing the poverty line". Narrowing is exactly what it is. That is not the fault of the minister, but until we find another way in which to index the GIS, we are not going to see those add-ons as doing little more than simply maintaining what we have got. What we have got, as the minister indicated, are thousands of people below the poverty line, and in this particular instance most of them women.
It is time that the ministry, the department and any incumbent minister gave thought to changing the index that is used for the GIS. The consumer price index, which is the index that is used, does not any longer, if it ever did, have any relevance to the particular group of people we are talking about.

Thank you. Let me emphasize that if I can. If you look at the CPI March-April of this year, here is the breakdown for incomes. Think of all the people over the age of 65 that you know and have some sense of how they split up their budget. Food, 21.5 per cent; housing, 34.1 per cent-not in my city-clothing, 10.1 per cent; transportation, 15.8 per cent; health and dental care, 4 per cent; recreation and reading, 8.3 per cent; tobacco and alcohol, 6.2 per cent.
Whatever deficiencies the CPI may have or whatever value it may have as an index for other things, for people over the age of 65, indeed I would argue for people over the age of 55, those getting the GIS, whether we move it below 65 or maintain it at and above, we need a new index. The CPI does not fit our need any longer. The simple reason is that clothing, housing and food increase faster in our society than the other items in the CPI. It is those items on which older Canadians are more dependent.

Despite the welcoming of this bill, and I know hon. members will pass it in a hurry, it is wise to remember that it is simply not an add-on but is in fact required in order to keep up where we have been below the poverty line. Indeed, the index we use is no longer applicable. We should have a new index. I do not know what you would call it, but it should be one that takes into consideration the actual living realities of older Canadians and where they live.
There is another area I want to comment on with respect to the bill and with respect to some of the remarks made by the minister. I was not impressed with that part of the Speech from the Throne which called for a national pensions conference. Generally speaking, I am in favour of conferences. At best, they bring people together who share a common concern. They can exchange views. That is always worth while.
The reason I have difficulty applauding this particular conference is that it is going to take the place of something that is very important, that is, a comprehensive review of pensions and the issues that surround pensions. One of the things in the world of might-have-been's which 1 thought was useful, and hoped the new government would have carried on, was that the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs had been empowered by all-party agreement to investigate and make recommendations to the House with respect to issues dealing with pensions generally, in short a comprehensive approach.
At that time, as I recall, there were a number of people, both privately and in the House I might add, who said, "More reports! More meetings! Where is the legislation? Why more reports?" 1 explained at that time, and 1 think it is still fair to say, that the purpose of the committee was not to create any new ones but to be able to synthesize those being done by a variety of other sources and bodies.
When the minister talks about the national pensions conference, 1 gather she sees that as the substitute for legislation. The first step to legislation was to put it in that standing committee. It seems that was the appropriate thing to do, because indeed the issues that surround pensions ought to be known to everyone now. An increase of $35 a month does not amount to a pensions policy, nor does the holding of a conference. The issues have to be dealt with. Those issues are as follows.
First, the actual on-street economic and financial situation for many older Canadians, both below and above 65 years of age, which they find themselves facing. The minister quoted, although she did not identify the page, from the report "Women and Poverty", a report by the National Council of Welfare. On page 12 of that report you will find a description of a 67-year-old woman known as Mary S. It really is a good insight into the kind of reality these people face. It points out that the biggest enemy for these people is not fear but loneliness. Other than that, there is a very good description of what it is like for many, many thousands of Canadians. I quote from the report:
-most poor women who live alone are over the age of 55. While a few are low-income women who never married and others are divorced or separated
Old Age Security Act
women getting inadequate support payments, the majority are widows who were left with very little on which to live after their husbands' death.
Here is the key, Mr. speaker. "In Canada, two out of every three elderly widows have incomes which are below the poverty line." I do not think it needs to be embellished as the first issue, as the description of the reality of where older Canadians exist. That says it, and no amount of statistics or reports will change that fact.
Second, somewhat implied by the first, is the level of protection provided to women by the pension system. The level of protection by both public and private pensions in this country is abysmal. Indeed, the Lazar report which was started some three years ago is a very lengthy report containing a number of recommendations as to what ought to be done with respect to pension systems, both public and private, for women in our society. Let me put it another way. If you want to be poor in this country, be old and be female, because your chances will increase dramatically and no amount of statistics will change that, either.
Third, the performance of the private sector. That is a strong issue, I think, because we have to do two things; we have to assess that performance as the Lazar report and some others too, and we also have to take that performance and measure it against the public systems which are available. While I am on that subject I might add that when we are talking about the performance of those private pensions we need, now as never before, a review of the Canada Pension Plan itself not only in relation to how we "access women" to it but, indeed, what we ought to do in the future in terms of its funding. This is a matter which is fast coming upon us-by the mid-eighties if we do not deal with it soon. Or, like too many things in this country, we will find we are playing catch-up ball with our own ball and bat.
The fourth issue is the introduction of greater flexibility in the age of retirement. That is one of the minister's reports coming in, I gather, from the Senate. Its progress is painfully slow but it is still coming from the Senate. I think it is part of the Croll report. Any policy which envisages flexibility with regard to mandatory retirement at the age of 65 will be welcomed by many people for a variety of reasons, and I do not think the minister need worry about the kind of support she might get in bringing forward a policy of that type.
Fifth, and something which is not talked about very often in conjunction with pensions because it is so often dealt with as a separate category, is the position of the disabled and handicapped in relation to pensions, not only the amount of money but even more particularly, to the disincentive which occurs as year after year both provinces and country and, 1 might add, municipalities, have done their best to handicap the disabled because the way we go about the funding of those pensions in relation to handicapped people does just that.
Sixth, the protection offered families of deceased persons and, seventh, maintaining the purchasing power of the benefits which are paid out. I did not invent any of that, Mr. Speaker.

Old Age Security Act
All one has to do is to become somewhat acquainted with the literature and some easy reading will do it. Get acquainted with the literature and you will change your perspective of what you ought to be doing both in this House and as a politician. If you knock on any door, and I can think of them in my own riding as I am sure you can, Mr. Speaker, and look inside and see how older Canadians are spending their days, you will know that not only should this bill be passed quickly but that the issues which I have listed ought not to be only the topics of another conference but that they should be brought forward to the House very quickly to be passed into law, pieces of legislation which would make us more proud than we ought to be today.

I associate myself also with the tone of certain remarks which both previous speakers made. Knowing, as they did, that this is the day after May 20, each of them pointed out that there are certain things we would not have in this country, certainly things that Canadians would not have from coast to coast, were it not for a strong federal government. Old age pensions, family allowances, medicare-just imagine what would be the plight of our people in relation to these programs if they had all been left to individual provinces. It took a national consensus brought to bear on national government to bring these things into being and they are examples of the fact that it is really worth while to have a national government, that it is really worth while to be Canadians.
I am also interested in the extent to which both the hon. members who have spoken ahead of me discussed the level of pensions as it relates to the poverty line. The Minister of
National Health and Welfare said that the whole aim of this bill, which she treats as interim legislation, is to narrow the gap between the income of pensioners and the poverty line. The hon. member for Rosedale recognized that as its goal but expressed dissatisfaction with the fact that it does not go very far toward closing that gap. As a matter of fact, I think it is high time-and 1 go along with the hon. member for Rosedale in this-that we found some other way of deciding the level of pensions than by relating them to the consumer price index.
1 say in all fairness to the hon. member for Rosedale that when he was minister of national health and welfare and I complained to him about the consumer price index not being a proper basis for the indexing of pensions, he agreed with me and said he would have the matter studied. In fact some studies did come out of that exchange, but I think we in this House ought to be hanging our heads in shame when it is being said here today that our pensioners for the most part are living below the poverty line.
The hon. member for Rosedale referred to times when it got down to 72 per cent or 68 per cent of the poverty line. The Minister of National Health and Welfare boasts that this legislation will bring certain of our pensioners up to 80 per cent of the poverty level and that, perhaps down the line a bit, they might even reach 85 per cent. The Minister of National Health and Welfare, in a mood of expansiveness, got to one point where she said that down the line somewhere married couples might even have 103 per cent of the poverty level. I would like to know how she arrived at that figure. It seemed to me that she was escalating the pension by the July 1 change which will take place, but she has overlooked the fact that the poverty line will probably have gone up in the meantime, so the likelihood of our getting the mass of our pensioners-50 per cent or 60 per cent of them-above the poverty line by this bill, or by anything that is before this session of Parliament, is very slim.
1 should like to suggest very strongly that we should turn our backs on this idea of pensioners being below the poverty line and that we should build into our legislation a requirement that no pensioner shall have anything less than 125 per cent of the poverty level.

What is wrong with that? It is not good enough just to keep people at the poverty level, just to keep our old people alive. Surely they are entitled to some measure of the enjoyment of life as they have made it possible.
May 21, 1980

1 remind the Elouse that we do use other indices in some cases. I put a question to the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. MacDonald) today about the rate of the disability pension. Actually, I was complaining that a formula which was arrived at in 1973 has not been made permanent and automatic. Nevertheless, the concept in the war disability pension is that the level of that pension for a 100 per cent disabled pensioner must be related to the average take-home pay of five designated categories in the public service. That formula does not talk about the consumer price index. That formula talks about a level of pay. Our problem is that in two or three years after it gets set it has slipped behind, but at least we have been able to persuade the government to introduce legislation to bring it up to date.
If i may mention another subject concerning which my remarks are not always popular, the subject of the pay of members of Parliament, we get an increase every January. Is it based on the consumer price index? No, it is based on the composite wage index, and we get up to 7 per cent if the composite wage index goes up to that point. So there are other arrangements and other payments which are based on something other than the consumer price index, and I agree with the hon. member for Rosedale that the use of that index for increasing pensions has been a failure. I have contended at times that part of the reason is that it is always behind. When you go back to get a three months' period two months ago and compare it with three months before that, and then get that increase a couple of months from now, you are getting an increase that the pensioners should have had six or eight months ago.
Another factor, of course, is that the consumer price index covers all the things which are in that package and is not directly related to the things pensioners have to buy. But even apart from those things I think the principle of indexing by the consumer price index-as though that solves the problem-is wrong. Of course, fundamentally the reason it is wrong is because the base was too low in the first place. But when I propose that the level of pensions should bear a relationship to the poverty line as established by Statistics Canada, we are at least talking about something which has some realism about it.
My colleague sitting next to me asked me a moment ago where this poverty line comes from, and 1 said to him, "Well, the poverty line that the other two speakers are using is the
Old Age Security Act
one published by Statistics Canada". It is, of course, the lowest of most of the poverty lines which are published. Ask any body of social workers or any group of social agencies in any of our cities for a poverty line. It will be a lot higher than the line put out by Statistics Canada. Senator Croll's committee over in the other place has established a poverty line a number of times and has updated it. All those poverty lines, as I say, are higher than the poverty line established by Statistics Canada.
That is one of the reasons I would not dare stand here and say that pensioners should be given a level of pension equal to the poverty line. That is just bare existence. It should be at least 125 per cent of the poverty line as set by Statistics Canada.
May I also point out that when Statistics Canada produces the poverty line, it does it for different kinds of areas. It does it for those who live in the rural parts of the country. It does it for those who live in small communities, small cities and small towns, and it moves up into the 100,000 to 500,000 cities and to the cities 500,000 and over. And, of course, the poverty line varies a great deal depending upon whether a pensioner is living in a rural area, in a small town, a medium-sized city, or in one of the larger cities of this country. As the Minister of National Health and Welfare will confirm, even with the increase she is now bringing in, this $35 increase per household, and even after the indexing takes place in July, it will still be a fact that for our single pensioners they will all be below Statistics Canada's poverty line for people in any of our urban areas.
Single persons who live out on farms or in rural areas may get pretty close to the poverty line by July 1, but the single people in our cities will still be below it. As for married couples, even though the improvement will be there so that some of them will reach the poverty line in smaller cities, if they live in Ottawa, Winnipeg, Edmonton, Toronto or Montreal, they will still be below it.
Perhaps I can continue this next time, Mr. Speaker. 1 see that it is six o'clock.
